query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-inducing a nanocrystalline near‐surface structure in the FeNiCrCoCu coating will promote the dynamic formation of an ultra‐refined tribofilm during high-temperature sliding, which in turn governs the overall wear resistance and limits plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate exhibiting a relatively coarse microstructure.
generation.intervention: A controlled pre-annealing treatment (e.g., hold at ~500 °C for a specified duration) to induce lattice refinement (nanotwins/grain refinement) before sliding tests.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding tests (e.g., in the range of 500–800 °C) under controlled load and sliding speed, ideally performed in an inert or low-oxidation environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of a dynamic, ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer (tribofilm) that forms by shear-induced refinement of the pre-annealed microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Controlled heat treatment promotes initial nanocrystallization which under high-temperature sliding undergoes further dynamic recrystallization and shear-induced refinement (exhibiting inverse Hall-Petch behavior). This refined tribofilm lowers effective shear strength, reduces material removal and crack initiation, and thereby enhances both wear resistance and mitigates microscopic plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the pre-annealed coating will show lower wear rates and reduced deformation (less severe plastic flow and microcracking) during high-temperature sliding.
generation.baseline: The conventional as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with a relatively coarse microstructure.
generation.boundary: These predictions are expected to hold in the high-temperature regime (approximately 500–800 °C) and under sliding conditions with limited oxidation; results may vary if the environment becomes highly oxidative or if the sliding parameters are significantly altered.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements and the interplay between the induced nanostructure and dynamic tribofilm formation need further empirical validation across different loads and sliding speeds.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical metal substrates: one in the as-deposited baseline state and one subjected to a pre-annealing treatment at ~500 °C to induce nanocrystalline features. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding tests (using, for instance, a tribometer at 700 °C under controlled load and sliding speed).
measurements: Wear rate (volume loss per unit load and sliding distance)
Post-test microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM) to assess the presence and characteristics of the shear-induced tribofilm
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-annealed, nanostructure-enhanced coating does not form a distinct ultra-nanocrystalline tribofilm and does not exhibit a significantly lower wear rate or reduced microscopic deformation compared to the baseline as-deposited coating under the same test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the longitudinal section morphology and element distribution of the matrix, transition layer and coating with 10 wt.% TiC. The three regions are clearly defined in the figure. The element distribution was analyzed from the substrate to the coating. From the matrix to the transition layer, the elements showed an obvious diffusion trend, which indicated that the formation of the molten pool enabled the movement and diffusion of each element atom during the cladding process, and the heat provided the kinetic energy for the atom movement. Therefore, the element bonding state was excellent, and could maintain perfect metallurgical bonding. In addition, Ti and C were uniformly dispersed in the coating, which increased the overall hardness of the coating. Figure 5 shows the hardness of the matrix and composite coatings with different TiC contents. The results showed that the hardness of the high-entropy alloy coating was greatly improved compared with the matrix. Moreover, with the increase in the TiC content, the hardness of the BCC phase and the TiC-agglomerated particles in the composite coating increased continuously.

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
